title: Gather Daily, Leave None Till Morning (the Manna Rule)
kjv_text: And Moses said, Let no man leave of it till the morning. Notwithstanding they hearkened not unto Moses; but some of them left of it until the morning, and it bred worms, and stank: and Moses was wroth with them.
summary: The manna in the wilderness had to be gathered daily and eaten the same day; what was hoarded 'bred worms and stank.' A law of daily dependence and against accumulation.
original_audience: Israel in the wilderness, fed by daily manna and taught daily reliance on God (with a double portion before the sabbath).
immediate_context: Exodus 16, the manna narrative; the rule teaches dependence and prefigures 'give us this day our daily bread.' A double portion is provided for the sabbath — the one permitted 'hoard.'
historical_context: The manna economy is the Bible's anti-accumulation parable: enough for today, nothing stored, no advantage to the strong gatherer ('he that gathered much had nothing over,' 16:18) — which Paul cites for economic equality (2 Cor 8:15). It is the scriptural opposite of a market in grain.
penalty: The hoarded portion spoils — 'bred worms, and stank.' The punishment is built into the bread.
exceptions: The sabbath double portion (Ex 16:22-26), which did not spoil — the one sanctioned store.
nt_passages: Matthew 6:11 — 'Give us this day our daily bread'
2 Corinthians 8:15 — 'he that had gathered much had nothing over,' cited for equality
Luke 12:16-21 — the rich fool who built bigger barns to hoard

internal_contradictions.issue: The manna rule is a divine argument *against* accumulation and *for* equal daily provision (2 Cor 8:15) — which the USOC inverts into a rationing-and-scarcity control while its prosperity clergy build exactly the bigger barns Luke 12 condemns.

usofc_implementation: The scriptural charter of the ration system. The Bureau of Daily Bread issues bread against the Manna platform on a same-day basis: rations must be collected and consumed the day they are issued (the anti-hoarding rule, 'lest it breed worms'), and unused allocation simply lapses — you cannot save, stockpile, or transfer. Tied to it is the 'Idleness Loaf' policy (only registered workers draw a full ration; cf. 2 Thess 3:10) and a holy-week suspension. A humane parable of daily provision becomes an instrument of daily dependence: no citizen can accumulate enough to be independent of the state for even a week — except the wealthy, whose 'sabbath double portion' exemptions never lapse.
constitutional_analogue: Rationing law fused with anti-hoarding decree; the same-day-lapse mechanic is a food-based social-credit throttle with no secular equivalent outside siege or famine command economies.
scene_ideas: The family's ration lapses because the mother was detained past sundown collecting it — a day's hunger as a bureaucratic side effect.
A black market in 'yesterday's bread' — the smell of the spoiled hoard as the smell of resistance.
The wealthy family's pantry, full and lawful under a 'sabbath double portion' exemption, glimpsed in Act 1 and understood only in Act 2.
satirical_uses: A parable against hoarding, run by a clergy that hoards, enforced against a people who cannot — 'daily bread' as a leash.
bureaucratic_uses: same-day ration issuance and lapse (the Manna platform)
sabbath double-portion exemptions for high tiers
